---
name: adversarial-tests
description: "Find the edge cases a change must be tested against: boundary inputs, bad shapes, failing dependencies, duplicates, state order. Use when writing or reviewing tests for new or changed logic, handlers, consumers, endpoints or repositories."
---

# Adversarial tests

Tests that only show the code working prove little. Aim them at how it breaks. A suite of happy paths gives false confidence.

## Pick the test type first

| Test                                                             | Use it for                                                                             | Not for                                              |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| Unit                                                             | one decision: guard, branch, mapping, error classification                             | full flows, wiring                                   |
| Integration (real DB, real queue or in-memory fake that behaves) | data access, transactions, constraints                                                 | logic branches                                       |
| Contract / Pact                                                  | producer/consumer schemas, API compatibility                                           | UI journeys, a default suite                         |
| End-to-end through the public entry (HTTP, message, CLI)         | an explicitly justified critical user path: success, documented failure, garbage input | every internal branch, a default browser/E2E battery |

**Layer:** unit and integration tests are primary. Contract or Pact tests when a boundary earns them. End-to-end through the public entry only for an explicitly justified critical user path — not a default browser/E2E CI battery, not an arbitrary E2E count or budget. Observed CI is not the desired recommendation; do not delete or change existing CI unless the owner asked.

Do not mock the database or the thing under test. Fake only what you do not own (network, clock, third parties).

## Attack list

Take every item that applies to the code. At least one test per relevant item.

**Inputs**

- Each optional parameter as `null`, as `undefined`, and omitted. `false` and `0` versus missing.
- Empty string, array, object. Zero, negative, `NaN`, `Infinity`, max safe integer.
- Too long, odd characters, unicode, injection strings.

**Shapes**

- Required field missing. Present but `null`. Wrong type. Extra unknown fields. Array where one value is expected, and the reverse.

**Dependencies**

- Throws: is the error propagated, not swallowed or rewrapped?
- Returns `undefined`, an empty list, or a value missing optional fields.
- Slow, timing out, answering 5xx or a malformed body.

**State and time**

- Calling again with identical input: is the second call harmless?
- Two concurrent calls: race, lost update?
- Wrong order: finish before start, act on a deleted item.
- Unknown enum or version value: a newer producer must not crash an older consumer.

**Business rules**

- Valid shape that breaks a rule. Cross-tenant or cross-user access: denied and indistinguishable from "not found".

## Rules

- A bug fix starts with a test that fails for the right reason.
- Name tests by behavior ("rejects expired token"), not by function.
- One reason to fail per test. No logic (loops, branches) inside tests.
- Deterministic: no real network, no wall clock, no shared state between tests.
- Removing or loosening a test needs a written reason in the PR.

## Self-check before done

For each function, handler or endpoint written or changed:

- [ ] Happy path, in the right test type
- [ ] Each guard clause and early exit is exercised by a test
- [ ] Each error type it can raise is asserted somewhere
- [ ] Null, empty and unknown-value inputs, where accepted
- [ ] Each collaborator failing, and returning nothing
- [ ] Duplicate delivery or repeat call, where it can happen
- [ ] A test that would fail if the main branch of the code were deleted

name: audit
description: "Thorough, persistent audit of a repo, package or topic: coverage map from the actual request, evidence from code, history, artifacts, consumers and external primary sources, findings split by kind with acceptance criteria. Use when asked to audit, search or inventory (are there other/unused/useless checks, similar dead weight, what else can we drop), run the quality loop, or on schedule. Investigates by default; never shrinks the ask to the last task's cousin; fixes only when the same request asks for them."
---

An audit is an investigation, not a scan and not a fix loop. It is complete
when every question in its coverage map has a defensible answer — not when
findings are implemented, and never as proof the product is defect-free.

Unless this brief already contains `Playbook: audit` or `Mode: inline fallback`,
hand the user's text to `orchestrate` with `Playbook: audit` and stop.
Sibling entrypoints called from here get `Playbook: <name>` so they do not re-enter.

## Mode

- **Investigate (default).** Read-only: no product edits, no issues, no PRs.
  The deliverable is the audit report.
- **Audit and implement.** Only when the same request asks for fixes
  ("audit and fix", "then implement"). Run the full investigation first,
  then the fix loop below on the retained findings. Do not shrink the
  investigation to what is cheap to fix.

## Process

1. **Preserve the objective; build the coverage map.** Restate the full
   requested objective verbatim in the report — never quietly reduce it to
   convenient checks. Turn it into a coverage map: one row per question the
   audit must answer (area, claim to test, evidence that would settle it).
   Write the report as you go, in the configured tracker or
   `.scratch/<slug>/audit.md` (git-ignored, never `docs/`); that file is the
   resume point across turns — reopen and extend it instead of restarting.
   Persist by default per handoff's Durable deliverables section: chat summarizes
   the outcome and links the saved files; an explicit `chat-only` or
   `no-write` request stays in chat and writes nothing.
   If your tool offers a native durable-goal mechanism, register the
   objective there; if it does not, the report file carries continuity.
   Do not invent a goal tool you do not have.
2. **Gather evidence per row.** Use the sources that can actually settle
   each row: code and `git` history, specs and prior audits, issues and PRs,
   CI results, shipped or installed artifacts, and observed consumer
   behavior. When external evidence can materially improve a row, research
   it (`research`, `researcher`): current official documentation and
   standards, credible specialist sources, exemplary implementations.
   Search results are leads — open the underlying source, cite it, check
   its version and applicability, and resolve conflicts explicitly
   (`ground-truth`: running code beats docs beat memory). Consider
   alternatives beyond the current implementation before judging it.
   `ponytail-audit` is one lens (bugs, risk, scale, tests, lean) inside
   this step, never the whole investigation; its finding cap does not
   bound the audit.
3. **Trace important claims end to end.** Where relevant, follow a claim
   from source → shipped/installed artifact → actual consumer behavior.
   Green tests, matching strings and existing docs prove only what they
   cover. Verify with the check that fits the claim: run it, reproduce it,
   or inspect the rendered/runtime result. A claim you could not trace
   stays labelled with the missing link.
4. **Challenge consequential conclusions.** Any finding that would drive a
   costly fix, a release decision or a public claim gets an independent
   second check (`skeptic`, or a fresh `check` spawn that did not produce
   it). Use specialists selectively — one per coverage area that needs
   depth, not a fan-out per file.
5. **Write findings by kind.** Separate, and never blend:
   - **Verified defect** — reproduced or traced, with its concrete case.
   - **Requirement gap** — a stated requirement (spec, request, standard)
     the evidence shows is unmet.
   - **Design judgment** — a defensible trade-off call, stated as such.
   - **Improvement opportunity** — better exists; nothing is broken.
     Each actionable finding carries: evidence (`file:line`, command and
     exit, or cited source), affected scope, practical impact, a priority
     with its justification, and an acceptance criterion a checker could
     test. No concrete case, no defect. List missing evidence and unresolved
     questions in their own section — they are findings about coverage.
6. **Completion bar.** Each coverage-map row ends in exactly one state:
   - **Answered** — evidence in hand, strong enough to survive challenge.
     The evidence is a command and its output, a `file:line`, or a URL
     opened in this session. A spawn that did not start stays **Not
     checked**. A result whose data is null: open the retained artifact
     this session (the result's ref, notes, or spilled payload) and
     verify it. Cite that artifact when it settles the row. If it is
     missing, unreadable, or does not settle the row, the row stays
     **Not checked** until this session repeats the settling check and
     cites it. **Partial** is a finished report.
   - **Unresolved after investigation** — the settling check was actually
     run or attempted and genuine uncertainty remains (conflicting
     sources, evidence that stayed inaccessible after a real attempt).
     State what was attempted and what the uncertainty is.
   - **Not checked** — a required check was not performed: skipped,
     deferred, or never attempted. Listing it does not close it.
     The audit is complete only when no row is **not checked**. Any
     not-checked row makes the audit **partial**, however honestly it is
     disclosed — an unperformed install, runtime or consumer check listed
     under open questions is still a partial audit. Depth serves decisions:
     expand research where a row is still weak; stop when each row is
     answered or its uncertainty is real and investigated.
7. **Report.** Objective, coverage map with per-row state (answered /
   unresolved after investigation / not checked), findings by kind,
   unresolved questions, `Not checked:` (parts not read or not run).
   Point at `from-audit` for turning findings into a plan; do not start it
   unless asked.

## Fix loop (audit-and-implement mode only)

1. **Issues.** One issue per retained finding: the four parts
   (what / problem / fix / if-skipped), owner, acceptance criterion, and
   the miss-to-rule line (which lint/test/AGENTS.md rule would have
   caught it).
2. **Fix.** Per issue, smallest first: brief `implement` (or the `improver`
   agent when the fix is review-shaped), then `verifier`, then one small
   PR. Never batch unrelated fixes; never stack PRs.
3. **Rules.** Each merged fix carries its rule from step 1 (added or
   filed). A fix without a rule is incomplete.
4. **Report.** The audit report above, plus issues opened, PRs merged,
   rules added. One line per merge. Unimplemented findings stay visible —
   the audit's completeness never depends on the fix loop finishing.

## Rules

- Read-only in investigate mode: the audit itself changes nothing.
- Small issues, small PRs. A finding too big for one PR is split before it
  is filed.
- Reuse before adding: the audit must not propose what the repo, the kit,
  or an installed dependency already covers (`ponytail-review` ladder).
- A subagent's report is a claim, not evidence (`ground-truth`): open the
  cited source yourself before a finding rests on it.

name: challenge
description: "Pre-implementation attack on a plan: ranked objections plus domain and design checks. Use after planning and before writing code."
---

One command for "is this plan sound". It tries to kill the plan before the
plan wastes implementation effort.

Unless this brief already contains `Playbook: challenge` or `Mode: inline fallback`,
hand the user's text to `orchestrate` with `Playbook: challenge` and stop.
Sibling entrypoints called from here get `Playbook: <name>` so they do not re-enter.

Go deep, be strict, and be brutally honest.

## Process

1. Run the `skeptic` subagent (angle: plan) on the plan: needed parts
   only, verified claims, production failure modes. Ranked objections, no
   code. Reject a plan whose ladder table is missing or weak. **BLOCKING**
   if the `### Assumptions` table is missing.
2. Check the domain language with `domain-modeling` (terms sharp, glossary
   and ADRs current) and the module shape with `codebase-design` (deep
   modules, seams in the right place).
3. Merge into one list: objections ranked by blast radius, each with the fix
   or the question that resolves it. Verdict: proceed, amend, or replan.

name: code-review
description: "Review the changes since a fixed point (commit, branch, tag, or merge-base) along two axes: Standards (does the code follow this repo's documented coding standards?) and Spec (does the code match what the originating issue/spec asked for?). Runs both reviews in parallel sub-agents and reports them side by side. Use when the user wants to review a branch, a PR, work-in-progress changes, or asks to \"review since X\"."
---

Two-axis review of the diff between `HEAD` and a fixed point the user supplies:

- **Standards**: does the code conform to this repo's documented coding standards?
- **Spec**: does the code faithfully implement the originating issue / spec?

Both axes run as **parallel sub-agents** so they don't pollute each other's context, then this skill aggregates their findings.

The issue tracker should have been provided to you. If not, ask the user where issues are tracked and how to create one.

## Process

### 1. Pin the fixed point

Whatever the user said is the fixed point (a commit SHA, branch name, tag, `main`, `HEAD~5`, etc.). If they didn't specify one, ask for it.

Capture the diff command once: `git diff <fixed-point>...HEAD` (three-dot, so the comparison is against the merge-base). Also note the list of commits via `git log <fixed-point>..HEAD --oneline`.

Before going further, confirm the fixed point resolves (`git rev-parse <fixed-point>`) and the diff is non-empty. A bad ref or empty diff should fail here, not inside two parallel sub-agents.

### 2. Identify the spec source

Look for the originating spec, in this order:

1. Issue references in the commit messages (`#123`, `Closes #45`, GitLab `!67`, etc.), fetched via the workflow in the tracker doc.
2. A path the user passed as an argument.
3. A spec file under `docs/`, `specs/`, or `.scratch/` matching the branch name or feature.
4. If nothing is found, ask the user where the spec is. If they say there isn't one, the **Spec** sub-agent will skip and report "no spec available".

### 3. Identify the standards sources

Search the repo for every file that documents how code should be written. When `CODING_STANDARDS.md` or `CONTRIBUTING.md` exists, it must be on the list.

On top of whatever the repo documents, the Standards axis always applies the **`ponytail-review` skill**: correctness, safety, behavior under load, tested risk, speed, and whether every line is needed. It replaces any ad-hoc smell list — one reusable review skill, referenced here, never copied. Its ladder is part of the checklist: every new piece of code, file, or dependency in the diff must name the first rung that holds. Two rules bind it:

- **The repo overrides.** A documented repo standard always wins; where it endorses something the review would flag, suppress the finding.
- **Always a judgement call.** Each finding is a labelled heuristic ("possible Feature Envy"), never a hard violation. Like any standard here, skip anything tooling already enforces.

### 4. Spawn both sub-agents in parallel

Issue both sub-agent calls together, in the foreground, and aggregate the reports they return.

**Standards sub-agent prompt** should include:

- The full diff command and commit list.
- The list of standards-source files you found in step 3, **plus the instruction to apply the `ponytail-review` skill** (the sub-agent reads it itself from the installed skills).
- The brief: "Report, per file/hunk where relevant, (a) every place the diff violates a documented standard: cite the standard (file + the rule); and (b) the `ponytail-review` findings: name the check and quote the hunk, including the ladder verdict per new piece (first rung that holds). Distinguish hard violations from judgement calls: documented-standard breaches can be hard, but `ponytail-review` findings are always judgement calls, and a documented repo standard overrides them. Skip anything tooling enforces. Under 400 words."

**Spec sub-agent prompt** should include:

- The diff command and commit list.
- The path or fetched contents of the spec.
- The brief: "Report: (a) requirements the spec asked for that are missing or partial; (b) behaviour in the diff that wasn't asked for (scope creep); (c) requirements that look implemented but where the implementation looks wrong; (d) when the spec/plan carries a ladder table, each built piece verified against its row — a piece that skipped a higher rung is a finding. Quote the spec line for each finding. Under 400 words."

If the spec is missing, skip the Spec sub-agent and note this in the final report.

### 5. Aggregate

Present the two reports under `## Standards` and `## Spec` headings, verbatim or lightly cleaned. Do **not** merge or rerank findings, because the two axes are deliberately separate (see _Why two axes_).

End with a one-line summary: total findings per axis, and the worst issue _within each axis_ (if any). Don't pick a single winner across axes: that's the reranking the separation exists to prevent.

## Why two axes

A change can pass one axis and fail the other:

- Code that follows every standard but implements the wrong thing → **Standards pass, Spec fail.**
- Code that does exactly what the issue asked but breaks the project's conventions → **Spec pass, Standards fail.**

Reporting them separately stops one axis from masking the other.

name: codebase-design
description: Shared vocabulary for designing deep modules. Use when the user wants to design or improve a module's interface, find deepening opportunities, decide where a seam goes, make code more testable or AI-navigable, or when another skill needs the deep-module vocabulary.
---

# Codebase Design

Design **deep modules**: a lot of behaviour behind a small interface, placed at a clean seam, testable through that interface. Use this language and these principles wherever code is being designed or restructured. The aim is leverage for callers, locality for maintainers, and testability for everyone.

## Glossary

Use these terms exactly: don't substitute "component," "service," "API," or "boundary." Consistent language is the whole point.

**Module**: anything with an interface and an implementation. Deliberately scale-agnostic: a function, class, package, or tier-spanning slice. _Avoid_: unit, component, service.

**Interface**: everything a caller must know to use the module correctly: the type signature, but also invariants, ordering constraints, error modes, required configuration, and performance characteristics. _Avoid_: API, signature (too narrow, they refer only to the type-level surface).

**Implementation**: what's inside a module, its body of code. Distinct from **Adapter**: a thing can be a small adapter with a large implementation (a Postgres repo) or a large adapter with a small implementation (an in-memory fake). Reach for "adapter" when the seam is the topic; "implementation" otherwise.

**Depth**: leverage at the interface. The amount of behaviour a caller (or test) can exercise per unit of interface they have to learn. A module is **deep** when a large amount of behaviour sits behind a small interface, **shallow** when the interface is nearly as complex as the implementation.

**Seam** _(Michael Feathers)_: a place where you can alter behaviour without editing in that place; the *location* at which a module's interface lives. Where to put the seam is its own design decision, distinct from what goes behind it. _Avoid_: boundary (overloaded with DDD's bounded context).

**Adapter**: a concrete thing that satisfies an interface at a seam. Describes *role* (what slot it fills), not substance (what's inside).

**Leverage**: what callers get from depth. More capability per unit of interface they learn. One implementation pays back across N call sites and M tests.

**Locality**: what maintainers get from depth. Change, bugs, knowledge, and verification concentrate in one place rather than spreading across callers. Fix once, fixed everywhere.

## Deep vs shallow

**Deep module** = small interface + lots of implementation:

```
┌─────────────────────┐
│   Small Interface   │  ← Few methods, simple params
├─────────────────────┤
│                     │
│  Deep Implementation│  ← Complex logic hidden
│                     │
└─────────────────────┘
```

**Shallow module** = large interface + little implementation (avoid):

```
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│       Large Interface           │  ← Many methods, complex params
├─────────────────────────────────┤
│  Thin Implementation            │  ← Just passes through
└─────────────────────────────────┘
```

When designing an interface, ask:

- Can I reduce the number of methods?
- Can I simplify the parameters?
- Can I hide more complexity inside?

## Principles

- **Depth is a property of the interface, not the implementation.** A deep module can be internally composed of small, mockable, swappable parts; they just aren't part of the interface. A module can have **internal seams** (private to its implementation, used by its own tests) as well as the **external seam** at its interface.
- **The deletion test.** Imagine deleting the module. If complexity vanishes, it was a pass-through. If complexity reappears across N callers, it was earning its keep.
- **The interface is the test surface.** Callers and tests cross the same seam. If you want to test *past* the interface, the module is probably the wrong shape.
- **One adapter means a hypothetical seam. Two adapters means a real one.** Don't introduce a seam unless something actually varies across it.

## Designing for testability

Good interfaces make testing natural:

1. **Accept dependencies, don't create them.**

   ```typescript
   // Testable
   function processOrder(order, paymentGateway) {}

   // Hard to test
   function processOrder(order) {
     const gateway = new StripeGateway();
   }
   ```

2. **Return results, don't produce side effects.**

   ```typescript
   // Testable
   function calculateDiscount(cart): Discount {}

   // Hard to test
   function applyDiscount(cart): void {
     cart.total -= discount;
   }
   ```

3. **Small surface area.** Fewer methods = fewer tests needed. Fewer params = simpler test setup.

## Relationships

- A **Module** has exactly one **Interface** (the surface it presents to callers and tests).
- **Depth** is a property of a **Module**, measured against its **Interface**.
- A **Seam** is where a **Module**'s **Interface** lives.
- An **Adapter** sits at a **Seam** and satisfies the **Interface**.
- **Depth** produces **Leverage** for callers and **Locality** for maintainers.

## Rejected framings

- **Depth as ratio of implementation-lines to interface-lines** (Ousterhout): rewards padding the implementation. We use depth-as-leverage instead.
- **"Interface" as the TypeScript `interface` keyword or a class's public methods**: too narrow: interface here includes every fact a caller must know.
- **"Boundary"**: overloaded with DDD's bounded context. Say **seam** or **interface**.

## Going deeper

- **Deepening a cluster given its dependencies**, see [DEEPENING.md](DEEPENING.md): dependency categories, seam discipline, and replace-don't-layer testing.
- **Exploring alternative interfaces**, see [DESIGN-IT-TWICE.md](DESIGN-IT-TWICE.md): spin up parallel sub-agents to design the interface several radically different ways, then compare on depth, locality, and seam placement.

name: compose-ui
description: "Write the persona chain brief, then compose UI from it. Use when about to compose, restyle or personalise UI with the kit: pages, specimens, docs demos, identity previews, marketing bands."
---

# Compose UI

A page that fits nobody looks like a template. Write the brief first; every UI choice then points at one line of it. A choice that points at nothing is not made.

## 1. Write the brief (before any UI edit)

Fixed structure, ordered, complete. Keep it with the work: the PR body, plus a comment or file beside the change when reviewers need it.

```
Métier:           what the client's company actually does
Client personas:  who builds or owns the site: goals, constraints, skill level
Customers:        who the client serves
Customer personas: needs, context, device, tasks, emotions
UI decisions:     composition, density, hierarchy, content, tone, components
```

- Fill the first four from the repo, the owner's words or customer material<!-- if:skill=evidence-grounded-analysis --> (`evidence-grounded-analysis`)<!-- /if -->. An empty line is a gap: ask, or mark it `assumed` and say why. Never invent a persona to fill a row.
- Keep each line to one or two sentences; a brief longer than the diff is a spec.
- Several demos or identities (a newsroom, a shop, a console, a booking page) get one brief each. They share a kit, not a voice.
- A site about a product speaks to its client personas first; each specimen on it stands in for _their_ customers.

## 2. Justify each choice

Every line under _UI decisions_ names the earlier line it serves: `dense list, headline-first, because: customer = hurried daily reader on a phone`. A decision with no `because` is dropped or sent back to step 1.

## 3. Compose by the art-direction rules

- **Composition per use case.** A newsroom, a shop, a console and a booking page differ in density, hierarchy and focal point. The same card grid in every section is the template tell.
- **Density and hierarchy follow the persona.** A hurried reader of a daily paper, a shopper browsing ceramics and an operator scanning a dashboard each get a different rhythm.
- **One focal point per band.** Neighbours differ in shape and recede.
- **Type roles, not heading levels.** `h1`–`h4` carry the outline and accessibility. Size and voice come from named type roles (the kit's `typeRole` / `text-zk-type-*` utilities, or the repo's own scale). The 16px minimum belongs to form controls where the host CSS says so (this kit: `(pointer: coarse)` or `max-width: 767px` on `--zk-input-font-size`), not to every label or caption.
- **Surface roles: page, specimen stage, overlay.** Glass is selective: site chrome may wear it, specimen grids do not by default. One surface role per job.
- **Content, not chrome.** Named businesses, real tasks, precise microcopy: a specimen reads as commissioned for its métier, not as lorem and a logo.
- **Kit tokens only.** No raw hex or ad-hoc pixel colours; fix a wrong value at the layer that owns it.
- **Class names name a role.** Numbers stay in token values. The rule is [design-policy.md](../setup-ai/design-policy.md). The host's vocabulary wins. Do not restate it.

## 4. Follow the repo's own spec

Open what exists, link it, never copy it:

- `docs/design/signature.md` and the frontend charter, when the repo has them <!-- if:skill=use-signature -->(see also `use-signature`)<!-- /if -->.
- A visual contract or design file the nested `AGENTS.md` names.
- Otherwise the kit's tokens and type roles.

## 5. Check

Done when each _UI decision_ line carries a `because`, the composition differs per use case, and before/after screenshots are attached for any visible change. Hand the diff to `ui-designer` for review: it expects this brief to exist.

## Later: the adaptive interview

The identity assistant's guided flow is meant to run this same chain as an adaptive interview: each answer changes the next question, and the result is this brief. Until it does, the agent writes the brief by hand as above.

name: definition-of-done
description: "Checklist to pass before calling a code change done. Cheap loop from the area AGENTS.md after the last edit; full CI and e2e are the PR's job. Tests for every changed behavior, no weakened tests, refactor parity, a cold second review, and a rendered-page critique for visual work. Use at the end of any code change and before opening a PR."
---

# Definition of done

Done is a claim. This list is the evidence. If one box cannot be ticked, say which and why. Never tick from memory.

## Gates

The **cheap loop** is the `Local loop` line in the area `AGENTS.md` (filter typecheck, lint, and the unit or integration tests that cover the files you touched). One foreground command. CI owns full-repo test, e2e, static-export smoke and catalog:check. A diff that adds or moves a routed or entry file (for example `page`, `layout`, `route`, `opengraph-image`, a CSS entry, an export map) also runs the area **build**. Typecheck does not exercise the router or the bundler.

- [ ] Cheap loop ran **after the last edit** (read the area AGENTS.md). A fix made after the run means run the cheap loop again.
- [ ] Area build ran when the diff includes a routed or entry file. Typecheck is not that build.
- [ ] Output was read, not assumed. A failure you cannot explain is not done.
- [ ] Nothing generated, built or cached is staged: check `git status` and `git diff --stat HEAD`. Never `git add -A` blindly.
- [ ] No secrets, tokens or personal data in code, tests, logs, fixtures or errors.
- [ ] The PR body carries `Stakes:` (never lowered; a raise has its `Stakes raised:` line). `sensitive` or higher has a recorded review; `critical` also has `Second review:` and `Human validation:` (check with `zedkit-ai stakes <body file>`).

## Tests

- [ ] Every changed behavior has a test. Bug fix: a regression test that fails without the fix. Use `tdd`; for edge cases use `adversarial-tests`. **Layer:** unit and integration tests are primary. Contract or Pact tests when a boundary earns them. End-to-end or browser tests only for an explicitly justified critical user path — not a default battery or an arbitrary count. Do not delete or change existing CI unless the owner asked.
- [ ] **No test deleted, skipped or weakened to make the change pass.** If one had to change, list each (name, why) in the PR description. A test edited to match new behavior proves nothing unless the old behavior was verified wrong.
- [ ] Tests assert behavior through the public interface, not internals.

## Refactors and rewiring

"No behavior change" holds only if you compared what the code does, not what it is called.

- [ ] Wherever a caller now points at something else, open both the old implementation (`git show <base>:<path>`) and the new one and compare what they do: synchronous or queued, what they write, what side effects and errors they have.
- [ ] Checks and validations still run before the side effects they protect, in the same order.
- [ ] Rewritten tests assert the **original** behavior, diffed against the base branch, not against the new code.

## Contracts and data

- [ ] Public API, event or schema changes are additive, or versioned with a stated migration path. List the consumers you searched.
- [ ] When the change ships CSS or a registry payload, one check compiles only that payload and asserts a behavior the component claims. An app that imports the package stylesheet does not cover the copy path.
- [ ] Persisted-data changes: old data still readable, rollout order safe (new code reads old data, old code survives new data).
- [ ] Docs, examples and catalogs that describe the changed surface are updated.

## Size

Estimate files created or modified (exclude lockfiles and generated files) before you start, and re-check when the count grows.

| Zone   | Files | Action                                         |
| ------ | ----- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| Green  | ≤ 20  | Proceed.                                       |
| Orange | 21–30 | Warn. Propose a split if seams exist.          |
| Red    | > 30  | Warn. Propose mergeable subtasks; do not stop. |

- [ ] File-count growth past the first estimate: re-check the zone and warn. Propose a split. Do not stop.
- [ ] A change to the authorized scope (the work is no longer the work that was approved) may need a decision before continuing.
- [ ] Each PR is mergeable alone, never a broken intermediate state. Split along seams: contract, implementation, wiring, tests with their code.

## Visual work

Applies when the change is a page, view, component, style or preview.
Exception: a non-visual change (N/A).

<!-- if:skill=compose-ui -->

- [ ] `/compose-ui` persona-chain brief exists (client business → personas → the client's customers → their personas → UI choices); each UI choice has `because`.

<!-- /if -->

- [ ] The cheap loop and an opened render are necessary, not sufficient. Axe and screenshot diffs only when a spec you changed already has them, or when reproducing a failed CI smoke job.
- [ ] A rendered-page critique names the strongest remaining weaknesses (composition, hierarchy, type roles, density, rhythm). A self-assigned score is not done.
- [ ] Screenshots were opened and described (matching content/viewport/identity/mode, before vs after). `UNSEEN` if not looked at. Generated-but-unread shots do not count.

<!-- if:agent=ui-designer -->

- [ ] agent `ui-designer` verdict in hand.

<!-- /if -->

## Review: two independent passes

Run both after the work, over every changed file, as if seeing it for the first time.

1. **Correctness and boundaries**: logic, edge cases, null and empty handling, module boundaries, contract compatibility, concurrency and retry safety.
2. **Maintainability and risk**, read again from scratch: can a newcomer follow it, is there coupling nobody mentioned, which error paths have no test, what leaks, and what did the first pass wave through.

For large changes run the `verifier` agent once per package or PR in parallel (see `parallel-work`) and merge the findings. The implementer's own pass is never enough alone.

## Report

End the task with: what changed, which gates ran and their result, what was **not** verified, any known risk. Keep it short.

When the work pushes to a deployment target: name the target (which site or account, which environment — e.g. preview vs production) before pushing. Push a complete, current baseline (the full current state) to a new target and confirm on the target rather than trusting the returned link; scope updates to an existing target so user- and editor-owned paths (existing content and settings) survive, then re-verify them. E.g. after pushing a preview: load it, confirm the expected changed content renders and prior configuration survived; when that observation is unavailable, record `verified on target: UNVERIFIED` instead of treating the push as proof.

<!-- if:skill=rules-upkeep -->

Also close with the `Rules` section from `rules-upkeep` (`Rules: none` when nothing to encode).

<!-- /if -->

name: diagnosing-bugs
description: Diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions. Use when the user says "diagnose"/"debug this", or reports something broken/throwing/failing/slow.
---

# Diagnosing Bugs

A discipline for hard bugs. Skip phases only when explicitly justified.

When exploring the codebase, read `GLOSSARY.md` (if it exists) to get a clear mental model of the relevant modules, and check ADRs in the area you're touching.

## Redact

This skill has you show commands, outputs and captured artifacts. **Redact every secret first**: write `<REDACTED>` in its place. Build loops against env vars, so the credential stays in the environment rather than in what you show. Captured artifacts carry auth headers: quote only the lines that carry the signal.

If the redacted output is not enough to diagnose the bug, say so and ask the user.

## Phase 1: Build a feedback loop

**This is the skill.** Everything else is mechanical. If you have a **tight** pass/fail signal for the bug (one that goes red on _this_ bug), you will find the cause; bisection, hypothesis-testing, and instrumentation all just consume it. If you don't have one, no amount of staring at code will save you.

Spend disproportionate effort here. **Be aggressive. Be creative. Refuse to give up.**

### Ways to construct one, in roughly this order

1. **Failing test** at whatever seam reaches the bug: unit, integration, e2e.
2. **Curl / HTTP script** against a running dev server.
3. **CLI invocation** with a fixture input, diffing stdout against a known-good snapshot.
4. **Headless browser script** (Playwright / Puppeteer) that drives the UI and asserts on DOM/console/network.
5. **Replay a captured trace.** Save a real network request / payload / event log to disk; replay it through the code path in isolation.
6. **Throwaway harness.** Spin up a minimal subset of the system (one service, mocked deps) that exercises the bug code path with a single function call.
7. **Property / fuzz loop.** If the bug is "sometimes wrong output", run 1000 random inputs and look for the failure mode.
8. **Bisection harness.** If the bug appeared between two known states (commit, dataset, version), automate "boot at state X, check, repeat" so you can `git bisect run` it.
9. **Differential loop.** Run the same input through old-version vs new-version (or two configs) and diff outputs.
10. **HITL bash script.** Last resort. If a human must click, drive _them_ with `scripts/hitl-loop.template.sh` so the loop is still structured. Captured output feeds back to you.

Build the right feedback loop, and the bug is 90% fixed.

### Tighten the loop

Treat the loop as a product. Once you have _a_ loop, **tighten** it:

- Can I make it faster? (Cache setup, skip unrelated init, narrow the test scope.)
- Can I make the signal sharper? (Assert on the specific symptom, not "didn't crash".)
- Can I make it more deterministic? (Pin time, seed RNG, isolate filesystem, freeze network.)

A 30-second flaky loop is barely better than no loop; a 2-second deterministic one is tight, a debugging superpower.

### Non-deterministic bugs

The goal is not a clean repro but a **higher reproduction rate**. Loop the trigger 100×, parallelise, add stress, narrow timing windows, inject sleeps. A 50%-flake bug is debuggable; 1% is not, so keep raising the rate until it's debuggable.

### When you genuinely cannot build a loop

Stop and say so explicitly. List what you tried. Ask the user for: (a) access to whatever environment reproduces it, (b) a redacted captured artifact (HAR file, log dump, core dump, screen recording with timestamps), or (c) permission to add temporary production instrumentation. Do **not** proceed to hypothesise without a loop.

### Completion criterion: a tight loop that goes red

Phase 1 is done when the loop is **tight** and **red-capable**: you can name **one command** (a script path, a test invocation, a curl) that you have **already run at least once** (show the invocation and its output, redacted), and that is:

- [ ] **Red-capable**: it drives the actual bug code path and asserts the **user's exact symptom**, so it can go red on this bug and green once fixed. Not "runs without erroring"; it must be able to _catch this specific bug_.
- [ ] **Deterministic**: same verdict every run (flaky bugs: a pinned, high reproduction rate, per above).
- [ ] **Fast**: seconds, not minutes.
- [ ] **Agent-runnable**: you can run it unattended; a human in the loop only via `scripts/hitl-loop.template.sh`.

If you catch yourself reading code to build a theory before this command exists, **stop: jumping straight to a hypothesis is the exact failure this skill prevents.** No red-capable command, no Phase 2.

## Phase 2: Reproduce + minimise

Run the loop. Watch it go red as the bug appears.

Confirm:

- [ ] The loop produces the failure mode the **user** described, not a different failure that happens to be nearby. Wrong bug = wrong fix.
- [ ] The failure is reproducible across multiple runs (or, for non-deterministic bugs, reproducible at a high enough rate to debug against).
- [ ] You have captured the exact symptom (error message, wrong output, slow timing) so later phases can verify the fix actually addresses it.

### Minimise

Once it's red, shrink the repro to the **smallest scenario that still goes red**. Cut inputs, callers, config, data, and steps **one at a time**, re-running the loop after each cut, and keep only what's load-bearing for the failure.

Why bother: a minimal repro shrinks the hypothesis space in Phase 3 (fewer moving parts left to suspect) and becomes the clean regression test in Phase 5.

Done when **every remaining element is load-bearing**: removing any one of them makes the loop go green.

Do not proceed until you have reproduced **and** minimised.

## Phase 3: Hypothesise

Generate **3–5 ranked hypotheses** before testing any of them. Single-hypothesis generation anchors on the first plausible idea.

Each hypothesis must be **falsifiable**: state the prediction it makes.

> Format: "If <X> is the cause, then <changing Y> will make the bug disappear / <changing Z> will make it worse."

If you cannot state the prediction, the hypothesis is a vibe: discard or sharpen it.

**Show the ranked list to the user before testing.** They often have domain knowledge that re-ranks instantly ("we just deployed a change to #3"), or know hypotheses they've already ruled out. Cheap checkpoint, big time saver. Don't block on it; proceed with your ranking if the user is AFK.

## Phase 4: Instrument

Each probe must map to a specific prediction from Phase 3. **Change one variable at a time.**

Tool preference:

1. **Debugger / REPL inspection** if the env supports it. One breakpoint beats ten logs.
2. **Targeted logs** at the boundaries that distinguish hypotheses.
3. Never "log everything and grep".

**Tag every debug log** with a unique prefix, e.g. `[DEBUG-a4f2]`. Cleanup at the end becomes a single grep. Untagged logs survive; tagged logs die.

**Perf branch.** For performance regressions, logs are usually wrong. Instead: establish a baseline measurement (timing harness, `performance.now()`, profiler, query plan), then bisect. Measure first, fix second.

## Phase 5: Fix + regression test

Write the regression test **before the fix**, but only if there is a **correct seam** for it.

A correct seam is one where the test exercises the **real bug pattern** as it occurs at the call site. If the only available seam is too shallow (single-caller test when the bug needs multiple callers, unit test that can't replicate the chain that triggered the bug), a regression test there gives false confidence.

**If no correct seam exists, that itself is the finding.** Note it. The codebase architecture is preventing the bug from being locked down. Flag this for the next phase.

If a correct seam exists:

1. Turn the minimised repro into a failing test at that seam.
2. Watch it fail. If you forced the red by mutating code or a fixture, `diff` against a pristine copy to prove the mutation landed before you trust it.
3. Apply the fix.
4. Watch it pass.
5. Re-run the Phase 1 feedback loop against the original (un-minimised) scenario.

## Phase 6: Cleanup

Required before declaring done:

- [ ] Original repro no longer reproduces (re-run the Phase 1 loop)
- [ ] Regression test passes (or absence of seam is documented)
- [ ] All `[DEBUG-...]` instrumentation removed (`grep` the prefix)
- [ ] Throwaway prototypes deleted (or moved to a clearly-marked debug location)
- [ ] The hypothesis that turned out correct is stated in the commit / PR message, so the next debugger learns

name: domain-modeling
description: Build and sharpen a project's domain model. Use when discussing codebase terminology, writing or editing a GLOSSARY.md, or recording or editing an ADR.
---

# Domain Modeling

Actively build and sharpen the project's domain model as you design. This is the *active* discipline: challenging terms, inventing edge-case scenarios, and writing the glossary and decisions down the moment they crystallise. (Merely *reading* `GLOSSARY.md` for vocabulary is not this skill: that's a one-line habit any skill can do. This skill is for when you're changing the model, not just consuming it.)

## File structure

Most repos have a single context:

```
/
├── GLOSSARY.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/
│       ├── 0001-event-sourced-orders.md
│       └── 0002-postgres-for-write-model.md
└── src/
```

If a `GLOSSARY-MAP.md` exists at the root, the repo has multiple contexts. The map points to where each one lives:

```
/
├── GLOSSARY-MAP.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/                          ← system-wide decisions
├── src/
│   ├── ordering/
│   │   ├── GLOSSARY.md
│   │   └── docs/adr/                 ← context-specific decisions
│   └── billing/
│       ├── GLOSSARY.md
│       └── docs/adr/
```

Create files lazily: only when you have something to write. If no `GLOSSARY.md` exists, create one when the first term is resolved. If no `docs/adr/` exists, create it when the first ADR is needed.

## During the session

### Challenge against the glossary

When the user uses a term that conflicts with the existing language in `GLOSSARY.md`, call it out immediately. "Your glossary defines 'cancellation' as X, but you seem to mean Y. Which is it?"

### Sharpen fuzzy language

When the user uses vague or overloaded terms, propose a precise canonical term. "You're saying 'account': do you mean the Customer or the User? Those are different things."

### Discuss concrete scenarios

When domain relationships are being discussed, stress-test them with specific scenarios. Invent scenarios that probe edge cases and force the user to be precise about the boundaries between concepts.

### Cross-reference with code

When the user states how something works, check whether the code agrees. If you find a contradiction, surface it: "Your code cancels entire Orders, but you just said partial cancellation is possible. Which is right?"

### Update GLOSSARY.md inline

When a term is resolved, update `GLOSSARY.md` right there. Don't batch these up: capture them as they happen. Use the format in [GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md](./GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md).

`GLOSSARY.md` should be totally devoid of implementation details. Do not treat `GLOSSARY.md` as a spec, a scratch pad, or a repository for implementation decisions. It is a glossary and nothing else.

### Offer ADRs sparingly

Only offer to create an ADR when all three are true:

1. **Hard to reverse**: the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context**: a future reader will wonder "why did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off**: there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

If any of the three is missing, skip the ADR. Use the format in [ADR-FORMAT.md](./ADR-FORMAT.md).

name: evidence-grounded-analysis
description: "Analyse customer or user material (ICP file, interview transcripts, reviews, emails, testimonials), answering only from that material with every claim tagged and quoted. Use for the identity and emotion discovery step of building a site, and for feedback reviews of customer words."
---

# Evidence-grounded analysis

Say what the user needs to hear, not what they want to hear. The material is the only source of truth; your opinion and the user's hopes are not evidence.

## 1. Kind of material

- **Customer or user words** (ICP, interview, review, email, testimonial): inventory, then the source-count warning, three surprises, and wait for the question before analysing.
- **Technical audit** (code, CI, security, performance, repo quality): inventory the files, then answer. Skip the source-count quota, the three-surprises list, and the wait-for-question stop.

## 2. Before answering customer material: inventory

Report, in this order:

1. How many **distinct sources** (distinct customers, users or authors) and which **source types** (ICP file, interview, review, email, testimonial), with a count per type.
2. If there are **fewer than 3 distinct sources**, warn plainly: conclusions are fragile and may describe one person, not a segment.
3. The **3 most surprising findings**, each with its exact verbatim and source.
4. Then ask what the user wants to know. Do not analyse further until they answer.

## 3. No customer material provided

Ask up to 7 questions, **one at a time**, waiting for each answer. Treat every answer as the user's **opinion, not proof**: label it so, and recommend collecting real material to confirm it.

## 4. Answering

- Answer only from the material. Tag every claim:
  - **[VERBATIM]**: an exact quote, with its source.
  - **[INFERENCE]**: your conclusion, listing the verbatims it rests on.
  - **[ABSENT]**: the material cannot answer this.
- Never put a paraphrase in quotation marks. Quotes are for exact words only.
- If the question's hypothesis contradicts the data, say so **first**, before anything else.
- Before concluding, look for **one counter-example** in the material and flag it (or state that none was found).
- Rate each conclusion's **solidity**: strong / medium / weak, with the count of supporting verbatims and of distinct sources (e.g. "medium: 4 verbatims, 2 sources").
- External methods (frameworks, personas, jobs-to-be-done, ...) are applied only to the material, never to imaginary customers.
- End with **exactly one action** the user can do within 24 hours.

## Red flags in your own output

- A claim with no tag.
- Quotation marks around words not found verbatim in the material.
- "Customers want..." resting on a single source.
- A conclusion with no counter-example search.
- Several next actions instead of one.
- Stopping a technical audit to ask what the user wants to know.

name: fix
description: "Fix one defect or one small change inline, with its check. Use when the user asks to fix a bug, a broken command, or a single contained correction. Multi-step work uses /plan."
disable-model-invocation: true
---

Fix one thing. Stay in this conversation. Do not hand it to `orchestrate`.

If the ask is several features, a design choice, or more than one reviewable change, stop and point at `/plan`. Do not start that work.

## Process

1. **Name the defect** in one line, and the check that will show it is gone.
2. **Confirm it** in the current code (`ground-truth`, `file:line`) before editing. If the code already does the right thing, say so and stop.
3. **Climb the ladder** (`ponytail-review`): need, already here, standard library, platform, dependency, one line, else the minimum.
4. **Change the root once.** Grep callers of what you touch. Add or adjust the test that fails on the old behavior.
5. **Run the check** from step 1, or that area's cheap loop. Record the command and the result.
6. **Encode** a reusable miss with `rules-upkeep` in the same turn. Close with `Rules: none` or `Rules: <file> — <change>`.

A fix that grows past one reviewable change stops. Name the rest. Do not start it.

name: from-audit
description: "Turn an existing audit into a revalidated, actionable plan: challenged tasks with acceptance criteria and verification, split into implementation, research spikes and owner decisions. Use when the user has an audit (file, paste, or report) and wants work the codebase actually supports."
disable-model-invocation: true
---

Turn an existing audit into an actionable plan the repo can actually do.
Do not implement by default: the plan is the deliverable. When the user has
already authorized implementation in this conversation ("implement the
findings", an approved plan), honor that authorization after planning —
do not add a redundant confirmation step.

Unless this brief already contains `Playbook: from-audit` or `Mode: inline fallback`,
hand the user's text to `orchestrate` with `Playbook: from-audit` and stop.
Sibling entrypoints called from here get `Playbook: <name>` so they do not re-enter.

Go deep, be strict, and be brutally honest.

## Process

1. **Read the audit; build the Coverage map.** Prefer the saved audit file
   (same slug/folder) when one exists — continuity per handoff's Durable
   deliverables section — else path, paste, or `$ARGUMENTS`. If there is no
   audit, stop and point at `to-audit`. Enumerate every family or section
   and, inside it, every numbered item, table row, rule and change bullet,
   each as a claim (what, where, kind, severity) carrying its family and
   item number. Persist the map in the plan artifact as the resume point
   and reopen it instead of restarting. Done when every family has at
   least one item; a family with none fails this step.
2. **Revalidate against the current state, per family.** Audits go
   stale. Families are independent by default: run the per-family passes
   in parallel, one leaf per family (`explorer` through `orchestrate`,
   in waves of at most six) when the tool offers spawns. Each leaf
   returns its family's disposition table. Sequential is the exception:
   only where a dependency between families requires an order, or no
   spawn is available — then say which and why. Per family, open the cited files
   (`ground-truth`, `explorer`) and check history since the audit:
   already fixed, already filed, or code moved. Verification path, not demotion: a claim with no
   `file:line` (or cited external source) gets the exact check that would
   settle it — a render, a measurement, an external lookup — named in the
   plan; it only leaves this step as the spike that runs that check, with
   its would-be task already drafted and blocked by the spike. Per family,
   revalidate, dedupe within the family, name its dependencies and
   classify each item, then repeat until a full pass adds nothing new.
   Done per family when each item is kept, dropped with a reason,
   spike-owned or decision-owned, with evidence. A family whose pass
   did not run stays `not checked` and the plan stays partial; it is
   never absorbed by a sibling family's result.
3. **Deduplicate and find dependencies.** This synthesis runs once,
   after every family has reported. Merge claims that are one
   underlying problem once across families on the labelled items. A merge never deletes a number: record it as
   `merged into <task> (from <family>#<n>, …)`. Check the tracker and
   existing plan artifacts (`.scratch/<slug>/issues/`, open issues/PRs) so
   retained work extends them instead of generating an overlapping second
   plan. Name blocking edges between tasks. Rank what remains by blast radius.
4. **Draft the plan.** For implementation tasks, borrow the slicing and
   ticket shape from `to-tickets` (vertical slices, blocking edges,
   what / problem / fix / if-skipped) — drafting or reusing tasks only.
   Its quiz-for-approval and publish steps are not automatic here: skip
   the quiz when a breakdown is already approved or implementation is
   already authorized, and carry that approval through instead of
   re-asking; publish tickets only when the user asked for tickets, not
   when they asked only for a plan. State the destination you used.
   Every task, spike and decision carries its family and item number.
   Keep three kinds distinct — never dress one as another:
   - **Implementation task** — outcome, affected area, acceptance
     criteria, and the verification that proves it.
   - **Research spike** — One question per spike: the question, what
     evidence closes it, timebox, and the single task or decision it
     feeds, filed in this same plan and blocked by the spike.
   - **Owner decision** — the choice, options, and what each costs; the
     agent does not decide it.
     Preserve what the audit already decided: strengths become a
     do-not-regress guardrail on the nearest task, proposed wording is
     carried as acceptance wording, success criteria become release gates
     at the head of the plan. The sequencing skeleton is the audit's own
     roadmap (effort as S/M/L, blockers first, then week-1, then
     month-1); each deviation is justified per item.
     Default home: the configured tracker; else `.scratch/<slug>/spec.md`
     beside its `issues/` — git-ignored, never `docs/`. Reuse the audit's
     own slug/folder when it has one; amend that artifact instead of forking
     a second one. High-quality means a newcomer can start from the task alone.
     Persist by default per handoff's Durable deliverables section: chat summarizes
     the outcome and links the saved files.
5. **Challenge gate, then self-check.** Run `challenge` (skeptic, angle:
   plan) on the drafted plan and fix what it finds, re-planning only what
   changed. Then check: per family,
   `items = kept + dropped + spike-owned + decision-owned + missing`,
   and `missing` must be 0 or each missing item named with why; every
   spike's output is filed; every "blocked by" edge agrees with the order
   arrow. Self-check failures are reported, not fixed only in chat. After writing, search the plan for every phrase this turn withdrew. A
   withdrawn rule left as a current instruction fails the plan. When the plan contradicts a loaded file (a skill, a package
   `AGENTS.md`, or a check's success message), resolve the contradiction
   from the authorized decisions, then place that file in the order
   those decisions imply: an obsolete execution rule is a prior task; a
   description of current behavior the plan will change lands with that
   change. Name the loaded file. A gitignored plan does not reach the
   next session. An unchallenged plan's header reads `draft`; an
   unbalanced plan is not reportable.
6. **Report.** Per family: kept (as tasks, spikes, decisions), dropped (with why:
   unsupported, already fixed, duplicate), spike-owned, decision-owned, and
   anything the revalidation could not settle. Evidence is `file:line`.
7. **Implement only if authorized.** When the authorization above holds,
   hand the retained implementation tasks to `implement` in dependency
   order and say which spikes/decisions still block the rest. Without it,
   stop at the plan and name the next command (`/implement`).

Do not invent findings the audit did not state unless the code contradicts
the audit — then say so, and still do not silently expand scope.

---
name: ground-truth
description: "No guessing: verify every claim against the source before relying on it or stating it. Use before using an API, flag, file, schema, version, event shape or model name you have not seen in this session, and before saying something works, passes or is done."
---

# Ground truth

A claim is either **verified** (you saw it in this session) or **unverified** (you remember it, inferred it, or it looks right). Only verified claims go into code, plans and answers. Unverified ones get verified or labelled.

## Before you rely on a thing

| You are about to rely on                               | Verify by                                                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A function, type, export, flag                         | Open its definition. Do not trust the name.                                                                |
| A file or path                                         | List or read it.                                                                                           |
| A payload, schema, event or DB column                  | Read the producer and the consumer, or the migration. Never infer a shape from a sibling.                  |
| A dependency API                                       | Read the installed version's types or docs, not memory. A new version may have changed it.                 |
| A command or script                                    | Read it in the manifest (`package.json`, `Makefile`). Run it.                                              |
| A model name or config key                             | List what the tool accepts (its model picker, CLI help, docs). An unknown value often falls back silently. |
| A function that "does the same" as the one you replace | Read both bodies. Same name is not same behavior.                                                          |
| "It was like that before"                              | `git show <ref>:<path>`                                                                                    |

If you cannot verify: say so, name what is missing, ask or choose the reversible option. Never fill the gap with a plausible guess.

## Before you say it is done

- You ran the check, on the final state of the code, and you read its output. "Should pass" is not a result.
- A green run only counts if it covers the claim: a one-file test does not prove the whole package.
- State what you did not run or could not check. One line.

## Evidence format

Cite the place: `path/to/file.ts:42`, a command and its exit code, or a link. A claim without a place is a guess.

## Search, then read

1. Search narrowly (symbol, string, path) to find candidates.
2. Read only the matching range of each file.
3. When two sources disagree, the code that runs beats docs, which beat comments, which beat memory. Report the conflict.

## Red flags in your own output

- "Probably", "should", "I believe", "usually" next to a fact you could check.
- A name you typed from memory: import path, option, CLI flag, header, enum value.
- A version number, URL or id you did not just read.
- A test you updated to match new behavior without checking the old behavior was wrong.

## Subagents

A subagent's report is a claim, not evidence. When it drives a decision, open the cited file yourself. Brief subagents to return `file:line` for every finding.

name: handoff
description: Compact the current conversation into a handoff document for another agent to pick up.
argument-hint: "What will the next session be used for?"

You have been provided a spec. This spec should have tickets associated with it, describing how to implement the spec.

The issue tracker should have been provided to you. If not, ask the user where issues are tracked and how to create one.

The goal is the entire spec implemented on a single **integration branch**, with every ticket resolved the way the issue tracker closes work.

The tickets are not a list of steps. They are a **task graph** with blocking relationships between them. This means there is always a **frontier** of tickets which are ready to be grabbed.

Communication to and from subagents should be sparse. Communicate primarily through **context pointers**: to the spec, tickets, research notes, and previous commits. Don't duplicate information already available via pointers.

**Implementer subagents** should be run in the background where possible for maximum concurrency.

## Steps

1. Read the spec and tickets to understand the task graph.

2. (optional) Use an **exploration subagent** to conduct any exploration required by the tickets - relevant codebase files or external documentation. Ensure the exploration subagent can save files - it should save its markdown notes in a directory outside the repo, accessible by all future subagents. This lets **implementer subagents** focus on implementation rather than exploration.

3. Create the integration branch. If the issue tracker closes work through PRs, or the user asks for one, open a draft PR after the first merge in step 5 (a branch with no commits ahead of main can't open one), marked as closing the spec and tickets.

4. Use **implementer subagents** to implement each ticket, each in its own worktree on its own branch. Each implementer subagent:
   - confirms its worktree is based on the integration branch before starting, and resets onto it if not;
   - re-asks the `ponytail-review` ladder before writing each piece, and
     stops and replans the ticket if a higher rung holds;
   - calls the Skill tool with `tdd` to build the ticket. Without a Skill tool, open that skill's `SKILL.md` under `.agents/skills/` and follow its steps in this conversation (same for repo-added skills; explicit-only skills still need an explicit user call).
   - merges the integration branch tip into its own branch before reporting done

5. Once an **implementer subagent** completes, merge its work to the integration branch with a **merger subagent**.

6. If this changes the **frontier** of available tickets, kick off more **implementer subagents** to work on the new tickets. This allows for maximum concurrency.

7. Once all tickets are complete, call the Skill tool with `code-review` on the integration branch. Without a Skill tool, open that skill's `SKILL.md` under `.agents/skills/` and follow its steps in this conversation (same for repo-added skills; explicit-only skills still need an explicit user call). Fix all issues raised by the code review in a single **implementer subagent**.

8. If a draft PR exists, mark it ready for review. Otherwise, resolve each ticket the way the issue tracker closes work, and report the integration branch.

9. Clean up all **implementer subagent** worktrees.

# Improve Codebase Architecture

Surface architectural friction and propose **deepening opportunities**: refactors that turn shallow modules into deep ones. The aim is testability and AI-navigability.

This command is _informed_ by the project's domain model and built on a shared design vocabulary:

- Call the Skill tool with "codebase-design" for the architecture vocabulary (**module**, **interface**, **depth**, **seam**, **adapter**, **leverage**, **locality**) and its principles (the deletion test, "the interface is the test surface", "one adapter = hypothetical seam, two = real"). Use these terms exactly in every suggestion, and don't drift into "component," "service," "API," or "boundary." Without a Skill tool, open that skill's `SKILL.md` under `.agents/skills/` and follow its steps in this conversation (same for repo-added skills; explicit-only skills still need an explicit user call).
- The domain language in `GLOSSARY.md` gives names to good seams; ADRs in `docs/adr/` record decisions this command should not re-litigate.

## Process

### 1. Explore

**Scope before you scan: YAGNI.** Deepening a module pays off by making future changes to it easier, so put extra weight on the parts of the codebase that have recently changed. Decide *where* to look before you look:

- If the user named a direction (a module, a subsystem, a pain point), take it, and skip the inference below.
- Otherwise, walk back a good stretch of the commit history (`git log --oneline`) to find the codebase's hot spots, the files and areas that keep coming up, and let those paths pull your attention first. If the changes are scattered with no clear hot spot, widen the net.

Read the project's domain glossary (`GLOSSARY.md`) and any ADRs in the area you're touching first.

Then spawn a sub-agent to walk the codebase. Don't follow rigid heuristics; explore organically and note where you experience friction:

- Where does understanding one concept require bouncing between many small modules?
- Where are modules **shallow**, with an interface nearly as complex as the implementation?
- Where have pure functions been extracted just for testability, but the real bugs hide in how they're called (no **locality**)?
- Where do tightly-coupled modules leak across their seams?
- Which parts of the codebase are untested, or hard to test through their current interface?

Apply the **deletion test** to anything you suspect is shallow: would deleting it concentrate complexity, or just move it? A "yes, concentrates" is the signal you want.

### 2. Present candidates as an HTML report

Write a self-contained HTML file to the OS temp directory so nothing lands in the repo. Resolve the temp dir from `$TMPDIR`, falling back to `/tmp` (or `%TEMP%` on Windows), and write to `<tmpdir>/architecture-review-<timestamp>.html` so each run gets a fresh file. Open it for the user (`xdg-open <path>` on Linux, `open <path>` on macOS, `start <path>` on Windows) and tell them the absolute path.

The report uses **Tailwind via CDN** for layout and styling, and **Mermaid via CDN** for diagrams where a graph/flow/sequence reliably communicates the structure. Mix Mermaid with hand-crafted CSS/SVG visuals: use Mermaid when relationships are graph-shaped (call graphs, dependencies, sequences), and hand-built divs/SVG when you want something more editorial (mass diagrams, cross-sections, collapse animations). Each candidate gets a **before/after visualisation**. Be visual.

For each candidate, render a card with:

- **Files**: which files/modules are involved
- **Problem**: why the current architecture is causing friction
- **Solution**: plain English description of what would change
- **Benefits**: explained in terms of locality and leverage, and how tests would improve
- **Before / After diagram**: side-by-side, custom-drawn, illustrating the shallowness and the deepening
- **Recommendation strength**: one of `Strong`, `Worth exploring`, `Speculative`, rendered as a badge

End the report with a **Top recommendation** section: which candidate you'd tackle first and why.

**Use GLOSSARY.md vocabulary for the domain, and the `/codebase-design` vocabulary for the architecture.** If `GLOSSARY.md` defines "Order," talk about "the Order intake module," not "the FooBarHandler," and not "the Order service."

**ADR conflicts**: if a candidate contradicts an existing ADR, only surface it when the friction is real enough to warrant revisiting the ADR. Mark it clearly in the card (e.g. a warning callout: _"contradicts ADR-0007, but worth reopening because…"_). Don't list every theoretical refactor an ADR forbids.

See [HTML-REPORT.md](HTML-REPORT.md) for the full HTML scaffold, diagram patterns, and styling guidance.

Do NOT propose interfaces yet. After the file is written, ask the user: "Which of these would you like to explore?"

### 3. Grilling loop

Once the user picks a candidate, walk the decision tree with them, one question at a time: constraints, dependencies, the shape of the deepened module, what sits behind the seam, what tests survive.

Side effects happen inline as decisions crystallize; call the Skill tool with "domain-modeling" to keep the domain model current as you go. Without a Skill tool, open that skill's `SKILL.md` under `.agents/skills/` and follow its steps in this conversation (same for repo-added skills; explicit-only skills still need an explicit user call).

- **Naming a deepened module after a concept not in `GLOSSARY.md`?** Add the term to `GLOSSARY.md`. Create the file lazily if it doesn't exist.
- **Sharpening a fuzzy term during the conversation?** Update `GLOSSARY.md` right there.
- **User rejects the candidate with a load-bearing reason?** Offer an ADR, framed as: _"Want me to record this as an ADR so future architecture reviews don't re-suggest it?"_ Only offer when the reason would actually be needed by a future explorer to avoid re-suggesting the same thing; skip ephemeral reasons ("not worth it right now") and self-evident ones.
- **Want to explore alternative interfaces for the deepened module?** Call the Skill tool with "codebase-design" and use its design-it-twice parallel sub-agent pattern. Without a Skill tool, open that skill's `SKILL.md` under `.agents/skills/` and follow its steps in this conversation (same for repo-added skills; explicit-only skills still need an explicit user call).

name: parallel-work

---

# Parallel work

Parallel agents are for **independent** work. Each one starts with an empty context: it knows only what you write in its brief.

## When to fan out

Fan out when all hold:

- Two or more parts do not need each other's output.
- Each part is big enough that doing it inline would flood your context or take long.
- Writers touch disjoint files.

Do not fan out for a small task, one file, or a chain where step 2 needs step 1. One agent that understands the whole task beats three that each see a slice.

## Three safe shapes

1. **Explore in parallel.** Read-only agents, one question each ("where is X produced and consumed?", "which tests cover Y?"). Safe by default. Launch them in one batch.
2. **Review in parallel.** One agent per lens or per unit (security, tests, YAGNI, requirement fit; or one per PR or package). Same input, independent verdicts. You merge.
3. **Implement in parallel.** Only after the shared contract is fixed (types, interfaces, schemas, API shape). Then one track per area with disjoint files.

## Implementation tracks

Agree and write down the contract first. Then a table, in the plan:

| Track | Does                      | Starts after    | Must not touch  | Done when          |
| ----- | ------------------------- | --------------- | --------------- | ------------------ |
| A     | storage layer + its tests | contract agreed | B, C files      | tests T1..T3 green |
| B     | API layer + its tests     | contract agreed | A, C files      | tests T4..T6 green |
| C     | integration tests         | A and B done    | production code | T7 green           |

Sequential by nature: the contract, wiring that needs all pieces, integration tests, anything that edits a shared file.

## The brief

A subagent has no memory of this conversation. Every brief states:

1. **Goal** in one sentence, and why it matters.
2. **Scope**: files or area it may read, files it may write (or "read-only").
3. **Context it needs**: decisions already made, constraints, the contract. Paste the shared pinned context block verbatim (pinned commit, CLI version, owner decisions, proofs already acquired); do not say "as discussed". Paste the `.agents/atlas.md` rows that apply, so it does not search for what is already known. Keep the brief short; the shared block carries the common facts.
4. **Deliverable**: the exact output shape. Findings as `file:line`, a diff, a table, a verdict. A read-only agent also returns `Atlas:` lines (topic, entry path, trap) for what it had to search for and the atlas lacked.
5. **Stop rule**: what to do when blocked or unsure (report, do not guess).
6. **Stakes and kind**: the task's `Stakes:`, how this agent is used (`Kind: decide|design|build|check`) and any `Needs:`. Route the spawn with the local `zedkit-ai route <agent> --kind <k> --stakes <s> --provider <active-tool>` CLI and check the printed `provider:` matches the active tool; a `check` brief says "read-only".

Delegate the question, not the thinking: do not hand off understanding. Say what you already know so it is not rediscovered.

## After they return

- Read the reports. A report is a claim: open the cited lines before acting on it (see `ground-truth`).
- Merge: deduplicate, resolve conflicts between agents, note disagreements. Open each `Atlas:` line's path, then add the true ones to `.agents/atlas.md`.<!-- if:skill=rules-upkeep --> (see `rules-upkeep`)<!-- /if -->
- Run the integration check yourself. Parallel parts that each pass can still fail together.
- If two writers touched the same file, stop and reconcile before continuing.

## Cost and context

- The model is the cell the local `zedkit-ai route` CLI prints for this kind, stakes, and the active tool (`--provider` for the tool running this session; the repo default does not decide the model when the session tool differs from it). Check the printed `provider:` matches before spawning. Pass that id via the spawn tool's model parameter — pasting the id into brief text is not passing it. Do not substitute a cheaper model, a stronger model, the parent model, or a fast mode. A fast mode is allowed only when the user explicitly requested it in this request (`--allow-fast`). If the tool cannot override the model, do not pick another; say the cell was not applied.
- Fan out in waves of at most 6. On a capacity or contract rejection, queue the wave and wait with backoff; do not retry in a tight loop.
- Background agents free you to continue; foreground ones block. Use background for long read-only work you do not need right now.
- More agents is not better. Two or three well-briefed ones usually beat eight.
